9.x: Jesus explicitly tells us to pray to the Father directly: “Our Father…”. The Father tells us to pray directly to Him as well: “CALL UNTO ME, and I will answer thee..” (Jer 33:3 KJV); “And CALL UNTO ME in the day of trouble..” (Ps 50:15 KJV); “Then shall ye CALL UPON ME, and ye shall go and PRAY UNTO ME..” (Jer 29:12 KJV). So why do many Catholics want to pray to whoever they want to? Throughout Scripture, God hates it when you ask someone else for help: “Woe to them that go down to EGYPT FOR HELP; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots.. But they LOOK NOT UNTO THE HOLY ONE (not three) of Israel, neither seek the LORD(YHWH)!” (Isa 31:1 KJV); “Yet ye have forsaken me, and served other gods: wherefore I will deliver you no more. GO AND CRY UNTO THE GODS which ye have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of your tribulation.” (Judges 10:13-14 KJV). “When men tell you to consult mediums and spiritists who whisper and mutter, SHOULDN’T A PEOPLE CONSULT THEIR GOD INSTEAD? WHY CONSULT THE DEAD ON BEHALF OF THE LIVING?” (Isa 8:19 BSB); “And the soul that turneth after such as have familiar spirits.. I will even set my face against that soul..” (Lev 20:6 KJV); “And Asa… was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet IN HIS DISEASE HE SOUGHT NOT TO THE LORD(YHWH), BUT TO THE PHYSICIANS.” (2 Chr 16:12 KJV). Theologically, a “god” is whatever a person relies on for ultimate help, protection, or guidance. If you are in a crisis and your first instinct is to “call upon” a being other than God, that being has (in that moment) replaced God’s role as your Primary Provider. If a person believes a saint or an image can hear them, process their request, and influence their life, they are attributing omniscience (all-knowing) and omnipresence (being everywhere) to that entity. Since only God possesses those attributes, giving them to a created being “replaces” the Creator with the creature, which is the biblical definition of idolatry (Rom 1:25). In Jeremiah 2:13, God defines idolatry as a two fold-evil: (1) Forsaken the “Fountain of Living Waters” (God); (2) Hewing out “Broken Cisterns” (other sources of help). If you have a direct line to the “True Vine” (Jesus), seeking a “branch” for help is logically redundant. To pray to a “broken cistern” is to suggest that the “Fountain” is either insufficient, unwilling to help, or too distant, ALL OF WHICH INSULT THE CHARACTER OF GOD. In the OT, sacrifice was the primary way to worship. In the NT, the “sacrifice of praise” and the “incense of prayer” replaced animal offerings: “Let my prayer be set forth before Thee as incense” (Ps 141:2 KJV); The prayers are in “golden vials” before the throne of God (Rev 5:8). If prayer is the “incense” of the NT, then offering that incense to anyone other than God is the spiritual equivalent of the “Strange Fire” offered by Nadab and Abihu (Lev 10), which resulted in their immediate death. It is taking what is “Holy to the LORD” and giving it to a common thing. “Prayer” is “Latria” (Lk 2:37), and we know that “Latria” is for God alone (Mt 4:10). The First Commandment says: “Thou shalt have no other gods BEFORE ME” (Ex 20:3 KJV). In Hebrew, “BEFORE ME” can mean “in my face” or “in my presence.” By bringing a request to a saint, an icon, or a medium while standing in the presence of an omnipresent God, the petitioner is essentially turning their back on the King to talk to a courtier. This replaces the Father-Only relationship (the babes) with a Client-Patron relationship, which God explicitly rejected in the prophets. If the Bible says to “CAST ALL YOUR CARE UPON HIM” (1 Peter 5:7 KJV), then keeping some cares back to give to a saint or an icon means you aren’t fully trusting God. In this light, any prayer directed elsewhere isn’t just a “supplement” to faith; it is a replacement for it. It suggests that God is not enough, and that “something else” is needed to bridge the gap - the very idea that led to the Iconoclastic War (~726-843AC) and the Ephesian Riot of Acts (Acts 19:23-41).

10.x: “Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven”: this request is not answered until the end times in the book of Revelation, where prayer is not just a conversation; it is a legal petition that eventually triggers the end of the world. In the throne room, the twenty-four elders (who probably represent all redeemed Christians = 12 tribes of Israel + 12 apostles) hold golden bowls (vials) filled with incense: “...having every one of them harps, and golden vials(bowls) full of odours, WHICH ARE THE PRAYERS OF SAINTS.” (Rev 5:8 KJV). At this stage, the prayers are being “stored” or presented, and just one chapter later, the “Fifth seal” is opened, and we see the “saints” whose prayers were in those bowls. They are located “under the altar”: the place where the blood of sacrifices was poured out in the OT: “...I saw under the altar the souls of them THAT WERE SLAIN FOR THE WORD OF GOD… And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” (Rev 6:9-10 KJV). These are the “prayers of the saints” claiming for “Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.” These prayers aren’t praying for general blessings; they are filing a formal, legal demand for justice and judgement against their killers. In Rev 8:3-5, we find that these prayers are the catalyst for God’s judgement. An angel takes the incense (the prayers) and offers them on the golden altar. The smoke of the prayers goes up before God & God “answers” the prayers by transforming them into the tools of destruction: “And the angel took the censer, and FILLED IT WITH FIRE OF THE ALTAR, AND CAST IT INTO THE EARTH: and there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake.” (Rev 8:3-5 KJV). Since absolutely no one in the Bible prays to a dead saint (except Saul who got killed by God for it), Catholics try to argue that the abstract text of Rev 5:8 justifies saint intercession. However, as we have seen, Revelation is not advocating for saint intercession, rather, it is symbolically portraying prayer as the legal request towards God that brings about His kingdom (and with it His judgement) upon the Earth. Taking Rev 5:8 literally to try to justify saint intercession would do serious violence to Scripture, and you would have to explain why there are only 24 elders and 4 beats with these golden vials (bowls).

11.x: “Give us this day our daily bread”: Jesus is teaching us dependence on God. We are taught to ask, not assume. This confesses that God is the giver of all things & that we are dependent on Him, not self-sufficient. “This day”: we are to trust God day to day, not to be consumed with anxious foresight, just like how Israel had to trust daily for the manna in the desert (Ex 16). “Daily bread”: represents the basic necessities of life: food, provision, sustenance. This does not refer to luxury. “Give us”: this is not a selfish prayer, but a communal one. It reminds us to care for others and to desire provision for all, not just ourselves.

12.x: “forgive us our debts”: Jesus is teaching us to ask for forgiveness DIRECTLY TO GOD, not to a sinful mediator man. We see this throughout Scripture: (1) “If we confess our sins, He (God) is faithful and just to forgive us our sins..” (1 Jn 1:9 KJV). John does not mention a priest, an icon, nor a saint. The transaction is between the “sinner” and the “faithful and just” God. (2) “I acknowledge MY SIN UNTO THEE(God)… I said, I WILL CONFESS MY TRANSGRESSION UNTO THE LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin” (Ps 32:5 KJV). When David committed his greatest sin (adultery and murder), he didn’t view his confession as a matter for a human religious system. He recognized that while he hurt people, the “theological” debt was owed strictly to the Creator. (3) “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy..” (Heb 4:16 KJV). (4) “there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). Only the sinless Jesus actually has a sacrifice to offer on our behalf, other sinful men have absolutely nothing to bargain for in our forgiveness of sins. (5) “My little children.. If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 Jn 2:1 KJV) A lawyer’s job is to stand before the judge on behalf of a client. John is saying that when we fail, we don’t have to hire a priest to speak for us - Jesus Christ himself is already in the courtroom of heaven standing up for us. THE ONLY SINS WE CAN FORGIVE ARE THE SINS COMMITTED AGAINST US: (1) “how oft shall my brother SIN AGAINST ME, and I forgive him? Till seven times? … Until seventy times seven” (Mt 18:21-22 KJV). Peter thought seven times was generous, but Jesus’ answer (490 times) was a way of saying, “Stop counting.” If we want our “lawyer” in heaven to be merciful to us, we must be merciful to our neighbors. (2) “as we forgive our debtors”: notice we can only forgive “our debtors”, not other people’s debt to God. The modern Catholic confessional box was not established until the 16th century due to constant sexual allegations. It was a way to protect modesty and to avoid more sexual scandals. “Private confession” was developed by Irish missionaries in the 7th century, and the Catholic Catechism admits this in paragraph 1447. The Catholic system is not apostolic.

13.x: “Lead us not into temptation”: the word translated “temptation” (Gk peirasmos) can indicate either temptation or testing (Mt 26:41). The meaning here most likely carries the sense of: “Allow us to be spared from difficult circumstances that would tempt us to sin”, similar to Mt 26:41 KJV: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Although God never directly tempts believers (Jms 1:13), he does sometimes lead them into situations that “test” them, like how Jesus & Job were tempted by the Devil (Mt 4:1; Job 1). In fact, trials and hardships will inevitably come to believers’ lives, and believers should “count it all joy” (Jms 1:2) when trials come, for they are strengthened by them (Jms 1:3-4). Nonetheless, believers should never pray to be brought into such situations but should pray to be delivered from them, for hardship and temptation make obedience more difficult and will sometimes result in sin. Believers should pray to be delivered from temptation (Lk 22:40,46) and led in “paths of righteousness” (Ps 23:3). “Deliver us from evil”: the phrase translated “evil” comes from “tou ponerou”, which can mean either “evil” or “the evil one,” namely Satan. The sense is to ask Him to rescue us from the power and influence of evil. “For thine is the kingdom..”: this last portion is not in Bibles based on the Critical Text (NIV, ESV, LSB, NASB, etc), it is only found in Bibles based on the Textus Receptus (KJV, NKJV, MEV, ReinaValera, WEB, etc). What that means is that it is present in almost 100% of the Gk manuscripts available EXCEPT in the two oldest ones from Alexandria: Sinaiticus & Vaticanus. Hence, leading scholars assume that it was a later liturgical addition. Whether this last part was added or not, it still would not constitute corruption, since the information is neither new nor false, and is elsewhere found in Scripture. For example: “Thine, O LORD, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty…” (1 Chr 29:11 KJV).

21.x: After Jesus warns against storing up earthly treasures, he reveals the psychological and spiritual reason why it matters so much: “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” Most people assume that our “treasure” (our money, time, and resources) follows our “heart” (our passions and love). However, Jesus teaches the exact opposite: THE HEART FOLLOWS THE INVESTMENT. He describes a spiritual law of gravity. Whatever you value most acts like a magnet for your emotions, anxieties, and thoughts. If your “treasure” is your reputation, your heart will be in a constant state of anxiety about what people think about you. If your “treasure” is money, your heart will be tied to the fluctuations of your income. If your “treasure” is heavenly things (kindness, justice, relationship with God), your heart will naturally drift toward godliness. This verse implies that you aren’t a slave to your feelings. If you want to care more about something, or someone, you can’t always “force” a feeling, but you can reallocate your resources. If you start investing your time, money, and energy into a specific cause or person, your heart will eventually follow that investment. You grow to love what you sacrifice for. Earthly treasures pull the compass of your life toward things that are temporary and fragile. Heavenly treasures pull you towards things that are eternal and secure. Be careful what you value, because you will eventually be possessed by the things you possess.

27.x: “Cubit”: a cubit (roughly 18 inches) was a standard unit of measurement based on the length of a forearm. “Stature”: the Greek word “helikia” can refer to physical height or the length of one’s life (age). So most modern Bibles translate this as: “Who.. can add a single hour to his life?” (BSB).

1-4.x: “Take heed… to be seen of them”: Jesus is not condemning good works, but the motive behind them. It is dangerous to fall in the trap of doing righteous acts in order to be noticed or seeking human approval instead of God’s. Earlier, he specifically told us to do good works for one specific purpose: so that they may glorify the Father (Mt 5:16). “Do not sound a trumpet… as the hypocrites do..”: hypocrites were those who acted outwardly righteous, but inwardly sought attention and praise. It comes from the Greek word “hypokrites”, which referred to Greek actors who wore different masks to play various roles. God does not reward hypocrisy, but he does punish it (Mt 23:13-22). In the Temple at this time, there were 13 collection boxes for alms called “shofarot” (שופרות). They were wide at the bottom and narrow at the top and resembled trumpets. These boxes made a recognizable sound as the coins were dropped in them, and often those who wished to boast would drop a large number of coins in at once. This was called "sounding the trumpet.” It was a practice of letting everyone know how much they were giving that Jesus opposed. “They have their reward”: the praise of men is all they will get, no reward from God, no treasures in heaven. “Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth”: give so quietly and sincerely that you do not dwell on it and there is no self-congratulation, as this would point to purity of heart & freedom from pride. “Thy Father which seeth in secret… shall reward thee openly”: God sees what others do not, and He values what is done in sincerity regardless of human praise. God will not forget to reward even the ones who simply give a “cup of cold water” (Mt 10:42) to one of his disciples. We’re not saved by works, and we’re all one body, so our works will vary significantly. The nose cannot do what the eyes do. And the liver is not as visible as the eyes, yet he’s still crucial for the survival of the body. So whatever we do for God, whether small or large in magnitude, we are called to do it in sincerity and love, not for praise. Jesus does not forbid public acts of charity, organized giving, nor visible good works, rather he is forbidding self-exalting motives. For God, the WHAT you do is not nearly as important as the WHY you do it.

5-6.x: “They love to pray… that they may be seen of men”: here the issue is not where they pray or how often they pray, but WHY they pray. These “hyporcrites” desired to be noticed as spiritual and used prayer as a performance. It’s important to clarify that Jesus is not forbidding public prayer. Jesus himself prayed publicly & the early church prayed together (Acts 4). The sin is praying to impress people, not to commune with God. “They have their reward”: just as before, they receive human admiration, but no reward from God. Their motive corrupts the offering towards God. “Enter into thy closet.. PRAY TO THY FATHER which is in secret”: closet means a private place away from human attention. Jesus is teaching that you should seek real communion with God, not public recognition. True prayer is personal, sincere, and God-focused. Notice how ALL PRAYER is directed at God. Absolutely no one in the Bible prayed to either a saint or Mary. The Bible is very explicit is teaching this: “CALL UPON ME in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me” (Ps 50:15 KJV); “Then shall ye CALL UPON ME, and ye shall go and PRAY UNTO ME, and I will hearken unto you” (Jer 29:12 KJV); “when thou prayest.. PRAY TO THY FATHER which is in secret” (Mt 6:6 KJV); “ye shall ASK THE FATHER in my name, he will give it you..” (Jn 16:23-24 KJV); “Giving thanks always for all things UNTO GOD AND THE FATHER in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph 5:20 KJV); “let your requests be made known UNTO GOD” (Phil 4:6 KJV), etc. And since Jesus is the Father incarnated, the apostles & early Christians prayed to Jesus directly: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Stephen in Acts 7:59 KJV); “For whosoever shall CALL UPON THE NAME OF THE LORD(contextually referring to Jesus) shall be saved” (Rom 10:13 KJV); “For this thing I BESOUGHT THE LORD thrice, that it might depart from me. And he[Jesus] said unto me, my grace is sufficient for three..” (2 Cor 12:8-9 KJV); “...Even so, come, Lord Jesus” (Rev 22:20 KJV). You will not find anyone throughout the Bible praying to anybody else but God/Jesus. The only person who talked to a dead saint was King Saul, and he had to use magic to summon Samuel from the dead (1 Sam 28). God killed him for it (1 Chr 10:13-14). Since there is no Biblical support for saint intercession in the Bible, Catholics try to resort to the most abstract and symbolic book of the Bible: Revelation 5:8: “the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb. Each one had a harp, and they were holding golden bowls full of incense, WHICH ARE THE PRAYERS OF THE SAINTS” (Rev 5:8 BSB). They argue that here we see saints holding the prayers of the saints in the golden bowls, and that they go before God to present your petitions. But to better understand this verse, we need to read Revelation in context. First, who are the living creatures and why do they have bowls of prayers as well? Second, are there only 24 saints interceding for us? Of course not, but these are all symbolic representations. For example, the four living creatures may represent God’s creation or attributes of His rule, and the 24 elders may represent the redeemed people of God, possibly the 12 tribes of Israel + 12 apostles, or the complete church across both Testaments. So the Catholic interpretation is already falling apart. Now, at this stage, we just know the bowls contain the prayer of the saints (believers). The identity and content of these prayers are revealed in the very next chapter. When the Fifth Seal is opened, we see exactly who these “saints” are and what they are praying for: “..I saw under the altar THE SOULS OF THEM THAT WERE SLAIN FOR THE WORD OF GOD… And they cried with a loud voice, saying, HOW LONG, O LORD, HOLY AND TRUE, DOST THOU NOT JUDGE AND AVENGE OUR BLOOD ON THEM THAT DWELL ON THE EARTH?” (Rev 6:9-10 KJV). These “souls under the altar” are the martyrs. Their prayer isn’t just a general greeting to God; it is a legal plea for judgement and vengeance. At this point, however, they’re told to wait until the number is fulfilled (Rev 6:11). In Rev 8, the scene comes full circle. The incense (prayers) is offered to God, and in response, the “judgement” they asked for is physically cast down to earth: “And another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the PRAYERS OF ALL SAINTS.. And the angel took the censer, and filled it with fire of the altar, and CAST IT INTO THE EARTH: and there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake.” (Rev 8:3-5 KJV). The logic flows like: (1) Bowls (5:8): the prayers are collected and stored; (2) Cry (6:10): the martyrs identify the content of the prayers: “Avenge our blood!”; (3) Judgement (8:5): God answers the prayers by turning the incense into fire and throwing it at the world. This is reminiscent of our daily prayers: “Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven” (Mt 6:10). God will answer these prayers in due time.

7-8.x: the Greek word behind “vain repetitions” is “battalogēsēte”, which comes from the Greek root “battos”, which means “to stutter.” Hence, the idea is to not repeat (or stutter) mindless formulas. Jesus is forbidding empty, mechanical, or manipulative prayer. He contrasts a true relationship with the Father vs a pagan-style prayer. Since Catholics include many repetitious prayer, they prefer to translate this verse as: “do not choose many words, as the pagans do” (Catholic Public Domain Version, published in 2009, based on the Catholic Latin Vulgate), or “do not babble as the pagans do” (Jerusalem Bible, the first Catholic Bible translated directly from the Greek in 1966, it is the first “decent” Catholic Bible), or “speak not much, as the heathens” (Douey-Rheims, English Catholic Bible translated from the Catholic Latin Vulgate as well, published in 1610), and they’ll try to argue that Jesus himself repeated prayer using Mt 26:44 KJV: “And he left them, and went away again, and prayed the third time, SAYING THE SAME WORDS” However, Jesus did not use repetition prayers like the formulas used in Catholicism, he simply prayed FOR THE SAME NEED three times, that is not the same as repeating a formula mindlessly. Also, his prayers are recorded, and they’re not exactly the same: Prayer 1 (v39): “O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt”. Prayer 2 (v 42): “O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done.” Prayer 3 (v 44): ‘“and prayed the third time, saying the same words.” Here we see Jesus presenting before the Father the same need, just like how we’re supposed to do ourselves. This is taught by Jesus with the story of the persistent widow in Luke 18:1-8, where he talks about a widow who continually approaches a corrupt judge for justice. Eventually, the judge gives in simply because she won’t stop bothering him. Jesus concludes: “And will not God bring about justice for his chosen ones, who CRY OUT TO HIM DAY AND NIGHT? (Lk 18:7). God expects a sincere prayer through a relationship with Him, you cannot force Him to answer through any repeated formula.

14-15.x: forgiving is a salvation issue. You cannot be saved if you cannot learn to forgive. Those who receive mercy must show mercy. Jesus gives a clear parable about this in Mt 18:21-25, where a servant owed his king 10,000 talents (an enormous, unpayable sum). The servant pleaded: “Have patience with me…”. THe master shows great mercy. He is moved with compassion and forgave his entire debt (not partial, but the entire unpayable sum of money). However, the same servant had a fellow servant who owed him 100 denarii (a very small amount in comparison). He grabs him, demands payment, refuses mercy, and casts him into prison. When the king heard of it, he said: “O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt.. Shouldest not thou also have had compassion?” (Mt 18:32-33 KVJ). Then he delivered him to torment until the unpayable debt could be repaid. The King represents God. The first servant is us. The unpayable debt is our sin before God, and the small debt is other people’s sins against us. So if God has forgiven an immeasurable debt, how can we refuse to forgive a small one? A forgiven man MUST (not buts) be a forgiving man.

16-18.x: Jesus continues to teach about true righteousness vs performative religiosity. Here is addressed fasting specifically. Jesus has already addressed giving (6:1-4) & praying (6:5-15), now he adds fasting. In all three cases, the issue is the same: doing religious acts “to be seen by men.” Jesus is correcting people who intentionally look miserable, disfigure their appearance, and make it obvious that they are fasting. He instructs us instead to “anoint thine head” (they used to comb their hair with oil), and to “wash thy face” (not to leave ash on your forehead). This is not about hiding spirituality, but about keeping it between you and God, not turning it into a performance to gain the praise of men. God rewards sincerity (the heart), not performance.

19-20.x: Jesus uses three specific examples of “decay” to show that physical wealth is temporary: (1) Moths: in the ancient world, high-quality clothing was a primary form of wealth. Moths could literally eat a person’s fortune; (2) Vermin or Rust: the Greek word is “brōsis” which refers to “eating away.” It suggests that whether it’s grain being eaten by rats or metal corroding, physical assets naturally degrade over time; (3) Thieves: even if the items don’t rot, they can be taken. In that era, homes were often made of mud-brick, making it easy for a thief to literally “dig through” a wall. Jesus contrasts “earthly” possessions with “heavenly” ones. Our aim should be acquiring real-state in heaven, not on earth. On the day of judgement, our works(not the person, as some try to argue this verse refers to Purgatory) will be tested “by fire” (1 Cor 3:15), where the fire isn’t meant to “punish” the person, but to “reveal” the truth and quality of our works. It will burn away the superficial, the selfish, and the insincere (Wood, Hay, Straw), leaving only what was done with pure motives and eternal values (God, Silver, Costly Stones) (1 Cor 3:12-15). That is our aim, not temporal earthly possessions.

22-23.x: Here Jesus addresses spiritual perception. In ancient thought, the eye wasn’t just seen as a sensor that received light, but as a window that determined how much light could enter the soul. “If thine eye be single” (KJV): The Greek word used here is “haplous,” which means “single, simple, uncomplicated”, something that is not doubled, folded, or mixed, but unified and straightforward. Its primary sense is “single, undivided” (as opposed to “double-minded” or divided in allegiance). Its extended sense is “simple, uncomplicated, sound, healthy, morally pure/generous”, depending on the context. So a better translation would be: “if your eye is healthy” (ESV). So if your eye is “healthy”(unobstructed with good perception) and focused on God, plenty of light will enter into your body and illuminate all your insides. “But if thine eye be EVIL” (KJV): the word used here is “ponēros”, which can mean “bad, cloudy, or even envious/stingy.” If your vision is clouded (obstructed) by greed or divided loyalties, you can’t see the path clearly and it will be hard for light to enter into your soul. However, since this whole context is about money, in Hebrew idiom, a “good eye” was a common expression for generosity, while an “evil eye” referred to stinginess or greed. For example: “He who has a GENEROUS EYE will be blessed, For he gives of his bread to the poor” (Prov 22:20 NKJV) & “Eat thou not the bread of him that hath AN EVIL EYE, neither desire thou his dainty meats” (Prov 23:6 KJV). So a rabbi might say: “If a person gives a gift, let him give it with a good eye,” that is, generously. Jesus is saying that the way you look at your possessions and the world, dictates your entire internal reality. If you look at the world through the lens of generosity, your “body” (your life) is full of light. If you look at the world through the lens of “I need more” (greed), your vision becomes distorted. You start seeing people as competition and objects rather than looking out for their well-being (only a true Hebrew author would know how to use Hebrew terms like this). “If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!”: Jesus warns against self-deception. The scariest kind of darkness is when a person thinks they are seeing clearly (walking in light), but their perspective is actually warped by materialism or pride. If your “moral compass” is broken, you don’t even know you’re lost. The NLT translates this portion as: “if the light you think you have is actually darkness, how deep that darkness is!”.

Mathew 6:24: This is the bottom line of the whole section. After discussing treasure, the heart, the eyes, Jesus moves to the ultimate question: Who is in charge in your life? In the ancient world, a servant or slave belonged exclusively to one owner. You couldn’t split your ultimate allegiance between two different masters with competing interests. Jesus isn’t saying it’s difficult to serve two masters; He is saying it is impossible. Eventually their orders will conflict. When God says “Give generously” and Money says “Hoard for security,” you have to choose which voice to obey. One will always be the “true” master, and the other will be the one you ignore. “Mammon”: the word often translated as “money” in modern Bibles comes from the Aramaic word Mammon. Mammon isn’t just “currency”; it represents wealth personified as a deity. It carries the idea of “that in which one trusts.” By using this specific word, Jesus is suggesting that money isn’t just a neutral tool, rather it has a “voice” and a “pull” that acts like a rival god. It promises security, power, and happiness, which are things only God can truly provide. Also, material wealth was often seen in Israel (and still today) as a sign of God’s blessing and a reward for obedience. But with wealth comes the danger of having a false sense of security or an erroneous assessment of spiritual standing before God. The heart represents the core of a person’s being, the real inner person. What a person values is driven by the nature of a person’s heart. Those who set their hearts to God set a healthy trajectory for discipleship.

25-26.x: Jesus addresses the universal human tendency toward anxiety, specifically regarding physical needs and survival. The passage begins with “Therefore”, linking it to the previous verse (v 24), which discusses the impossibility of serving two masters (God and Money). Jesus argues that worry is often a byproduct of divided loyalty. By commanding listeners “do not worry”, he is not suggesting that life is easy, but rather that anxiety is a futile response to the challenges of living. “Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment”: God has already given you the “greater” gifts of life and a physical body, so will He not also provide the “lesser” things required to sustain it, like food and clothing? If someone told you that they’d give you $10 million dollars with the condition that you give your life tomorrow, would you do it? Of course not, because your life is worth much more than all the money in the world. “The fowls of the air”: birds are active but not anxious. The point is not to encourage laziness, but to highlight that the ultimate source of sustenance is God’s providential care. “Are ye not much better than they?”: Humans are created in the image of God. If God ensures the survival of creatures that don’t share that unique status, it is logically inconsistent to believe that He would abandon His own children.

28-34.x: “Raiment” is an archaic word for clothing. “They toil not, neither do they spin”: Flowers do not labor in factories or work at spinning wheels to create their beauty; their “clothing” is a natural gift from God. The Solomon comparison: King Solomon was the wealthiest and most majestic king is Israel’s history. Yet, Jesus argues that a simple wildflower possesses a natural, organic beauty that surpasses the most expensive man-made fabrics. Hence, if God spends such creative energy on “grass” (which is temporary and used as fuel for overs) He will certainly provide for humans, who are eternal. Also, cut grass (a natural source for fuel in fire ovens) is a common metaphor for sudden serious changes of fortune and for human frailty and transience(lasting only for a little while, fleeting): “For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb” (Ps 37:2 KJV). “Seek ye first”: this is a command of displacement. You cannot simply “stop worrying” by willpower; you must replace worry with a higher pursuit. Even if someone manages to lose “unclean spirits”, you must fill it with God, otherwise the evil spirit will return & “taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first” (Mt 12:43-45 KJV). If a person removes a vice but does not replace it with a devotion to God, they leave a “vacuum”. And this vacuum is an invitation for even greater evil to enter. Also, worrying is a sign of little faith.
